name: Zenagamtide
lead: Zenagamtide, better known by the name amycretin, is an investigational once-weekly injectable and daily oral drug from Novo Nordisk that activates both the GLP-1 and amylin receptors within a single peptide molecule.[1][3] It is being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes and is not approved.[1][2]

In a phase 1b/2a trial of 125 adults with overweight or obesity running up to 36 weeks, subcutaneous amycretin was studied for safety, tolerability and weight effects.[1][3] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports a mean weight loss of 24.3 percent at the 60 mg weekly dose and gastrointestinal adverse events as the most common effects.[2] Phase 3 programs were reported to be planned or starting.[2]

paras: Amycretin is a single peptide that combines GLP-1-like and amylin-like activity. GLP-1 receptor activation affects appetite, while amylin activity is described as affecting satiety and gastric emptying.[1][2] In rodent studies amycretin was reported to reduce body weight and improve metabolic dysfunction.[5]

Grokipedia describes a 68-amino-acid peptide with a C18 diacid modification for albumin binding and reports a half-life of about 4 days for the injectable form.[2] The oral form uses the absorption enhancer salcaprozate sodium.[1]

Grokipedia reports that gastrointestinal effects such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were the most frequent, mostly mild to moderate, with injection-site reactions and some cases of dysesthesia in the injectable trial.[2]

A first-in-human phase 1 trial evaluated safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics of single and multiple ascending doses.[4] A phase 1b/2a randomised placebo-controlled trial studied subcutaneous amycretin for up to 36 weeks in participants with overweight or obesity.[3] Grokipedia reports 24.3 percent mean weight loss at 36 weeks in the 60 mg group, 13.1 percent at 12 weeks for the oral form in a phase 1 study, and an HbA1c reduction of 1.5 percent in a 36-week oral type 2 diabetes trial.[2] A phase 1 study of oral amycretin in Japanese men with obesity has been completed.[6] Commentary in the Lancet and reviews discuss the dual-agonist approach.[7][8]
Novo Nordisk announced phase 1 oral results in March 2024 and phase 1b/2a subcutaneous results in January 2025.[1] Grokipedia reports the oral form moved to phase 3 in 2025.[2]

timeline.event: Phase 1 results for oral amycretin announced.[1]
Phase 1b/2a subcutaneous results announced and published in the Lancet.[1][3]

card.summary: Novo Nordisk's investigational GLP-1 plus amylin dual agonist, with large weight-loss figures in early trials and no approval yet.
card.note: Not approved; reported gastrointestinal side effects.

quick.overview:
Zenagamtide is the name for amycretin, a single molecule that activates GLP-1 and amylin receptors. Novo Nordisk is developing weekly injectable and daily oral forms for obesity and diabetes.

Early trials were published in the Lancet in 2025; an AI-generated source reports up to about 24 percent weight loss at 36 weeks in the injectable trial.
quick.mechanism: It combines GLP-1 and amylin receptor activity in one peptide, acting on appetite, satiety and gastric emptying.
quick.risks: Gastrointestinal effects were the most common reported adverse events. It is investigational and not approved.
